MR. BURTON-ADEQUACY OF ANSWERS TO ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning answers to questions placed on the Order Paper. On October 23 I placed on the Order Paper a series of questions, Nos. 256 and 259 to 264 inclusive, asking for information about the designation of areas under the Regional Development Incentives Act. My questions concerned all provinces except the three maritime provinces which were completely included in designated areas. My first question with respect to each province was: "What criteria were used by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the selection of designated areas for the province... ". The answer provided to each question was: "Weighted measures of rates of economic growth (employment, income and population) and of potential for secondary industry"-a clear case of bureaucratic gobbledegook.
I then placed a motion for papers on the Order Paper asking for a copy of all correspondence between the government of Canada and each of the provinces regarding the selection of designated regions under the new Regional Development Incentives Act. The answer I received was that correspondence was exchanged only with the province of Alberta. This correspondence was subsequently tabled in the House of Commons and provided information on the views of both the government of Canada and the government of Alberta with respect to the designation of areas in that province. This was then followed by a series of questions in which I asked for information about the specific proposals placed before the government of each province by the government of Canada and the views of the provinces concerning these proposals. The standard answer submitted to each of these questions was that "the details of such consultations are confidential matters."
My question of privilege is that there has been a systematic attempt to evade the provision of information to which this House is entitled. Legislation passed by this House provided for consultations to take place with the provinces and now members are denied access to information on these consultations. We are told we have no right to know.
Furthermore, I submit that there is a conflict between the answer provided to questions 577 to 583 inclusive, and 596 to 598 inclusive, which indicated that the details of such consultations are confidential matters while the government had already provided full information on consultations with one province in response to motion for papers No. 140 concerning correspondence exchanged between the government of Canada and the government of Alberta. If it is possible to provide information on one province, how can the government hide behind confidentiality with respect to other provinces?
If Your Honour thinks there is a question of privilege I am prepared to move a motion to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for further consideration.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. BURTON-ADEQUACY OF ANSWERS TO ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS

In the circumstances I cannot put to the House the motion to which the hon. member referred a moment ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as part of the national effort to curb inflation the Prices and Incomes Commission is working to secure the support of the business community and professional groups for a program aimed at limiting price increases and charges for services. If meaningful progress can be made in this direction, this initial step will be followed by efforts to restrain increases in wages, salaries and other cost elements that affect prices. This will help to restore a balance between total money incomes and the total quantity of goods and services produced in the economy.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
It is important that major discretionary price changes in the Canadian market should be avoided while these discussions are taking place. Such price increases, even if planned well in advance, could easily be interpreted as being made in order to avoid the scrutiny which would follow the adoption of a program of price restraint.
With this in mind, the government has requested the copper producers and the railways to suspend the price changes announced around the turn of the year and they have agreed to do so. On behalf of the government, I have also had discussions with representatives of the two banks which had announced increases in their interest rates on instalment loans for consumers; they also have agreed to meet the government's request to suspend these increases.
I want to make it very clear that the government will adopt the same attitude toward any similar proposals to raise prices between now and March 1.

The Canadian Economy rise. If the minister wants to see this for himself, let him come with me along the commercial streets of Ottawa, Hull or any other Canadian city and see the special sales now on in every line of business, with some stores offering 40 or even 50 per cent oft their regular prices.
But the minister says that in order to stop inflation it is necessary to ask the Prices and Incomes Commission to get the support of the business world. And the minister states that, on the whole, balance between the purchasing power and available goods will be restored. What a misleading statement!
Mr. Speaker, why do the minister and the government tolerate, for example, that a province such as Quebec to finance Quebec Hydro should have to go and borrow $50 million in the United States at an interest rate of 10 per cent for a period of 25 years? The industrial sector in Canada is expanding very rapidly. Our corporate wealth has grown greatly. We in Canada have been able to develop industrially more rapidly than most countries, and possibly more uniformly. We have now reached the stage where we have a great corporate structure which almost supersedes government in the operation of our nation.
Several ministers were asked about the price of copper today. It was indicated that an arrangement had been made whereby a two-month stay on price increases would be retained. The decision was arrived at in spite of the great difficulty in deciding whether this applied to all the domestic producers in Canada, whether the copper consumers in Canada were all affected and how it would apply to the general public. This is an indication that our corporate structure in Canada has reached a level where it has more influence on the average person's life than has the federal government or the combination of the eleven governments which govern this country.

The minister is asking for all kinds of disclosures. He is asking us to look into the intricate dealings of corporations and companies. He has said we should look into them to the extent of knowing whether a shareholder is getting a fair shake from his company. The other day I was looking at some figures. I noticed that a company with a multi-million dollar investment, and stock running between $50 and $60, was paying a 71 cent dividend. I strongly suggest that a person having stock in that company, knowing the volume of business that company was doing and the expansion it has experienced,-would wonder why he was receiving a 71 cent dividend on a $50 share. It is 34 years since this act has been before us for major revision. Ten years ago, when four or five people were running the branch there was not much need for an 80-page act to enable them to deal with this operation, which was very small, inefficient, ineffectual. In Canada only a very small part of our corporate development has been brought about through use of the letters patent procedure. Most of the incorporation necessary has been done through special acts of Parliament. Over a period of years several members of this party-latterly, quite a number of us- have become interested in this incorporation procedure particularly as it affects finance companies, trust companies and insurance companies. The minister is now proposing to 
turn over to the companies branch authority to set up trust companies, finance companies and insurance companies by legislation.
Many of us are concerned about this policy. We are not opposed to companies being set up by letters patent. Mr. Speaker, this is an opportune time for the introduction of this bill. There are two things involved. First, we have reform of our taxation procedures as embodied in the white paper on taxation. This is very important to corporate structures as well as to the wide distribution of shares, profits and so on. If we have a faulty corporate structure, then the ideas expressed in the white paper on tax reform will not work. There is a great demand and need at the present time for reform of our laws regarding corporate structures. It seems that most of the people who want reform do not want change. This creates a great difficulty. We have thousands of experts who are knowledgeable in the old ways of doing things. No one is quite sure what the new way will be. Consequently, the old order has loyal friends and the new order has lukewarm friends at best.
It has been said that the minister has not gone far enough. I am sure he would like to go a lot further, but the minister has already gone further than his advisers have suggested. Like all presidents of corporations, I am

They suggest the minister should not go too far because the business community is very powerful and it should not be encouraged to move to southern climates. The bill itself is an indication that the minister will go a lot further. I suggest he could have gone further now but I am pleased that he has gone as far as he has.
Let us review the corporate image. I agree with hon. gentlemen opposite, especially those in the N.D.P., that most people picture a corporation as an individual who is corpulent, wearing a top hat, tuxedo and bow tie, and having dollar signs instead of eyes and ears. It is surprising how many Canadians have given personalities to corporations.
The corporate structure is the only feasible or workable method of participating in enterprise as it has developed in the world up to this point. This is a continuation of the English business community which created a personality without personal characteristics for corporations. In this way, people can invest money with limited liability. A corporation is nothing more than a group of investors who have limited their liability and act as an individual. It is for this reason the United States has become extremely powerful. This corporate structure has made great nations in this world. The lack of a corporate structure has been the nemesis of many nations. I have in mind France, particularly. It has never adopted the corporate structure method. The United States, England, Canada and Germany, to a great extent, as well as Japan, have accepted this system. It is still a good system, and I dare anyone to suggest something different which would accomplish the same thing.
There is a presumption that a corporation has a conscience. The late hon. Mr. Winters said that a corporation was expected to act as a good Canadian citizen. Of course, it is impossible for a corporation to act at all. For this reason, the conduct of corporations must be regulated to a great extent. Because a corporation has no conscience, it will make the last dollar wherever it can and it does not care how it makes it. That is taken for granted because a corporation has no ethics, no morals or personality. We recognize that corporations must be controlled and regulated, yet allowed to function within these regulations. We cannot presume that corporations are going to behave in any one way. They

will behave in accord with their purpose, and that is to make money through a limited corporate structure.

I should like to deal with the item of information. There has been a great deal of repercussion from this provision. I am sure the minister has had a great kick-back on the question of information, the financial information. I agree with this bill entirely. Whether the company be private or public, I cannot see the reason that it should hold certain parts of its activities secret. It deals under a public licence. It limits its liability under public law. If the officers of the company want secrecy, they can work entirely as individuals and be liable for everything they are worth. If they do not take advantage of the corporate structure, then they do not have to inform anyone. But I do not think they should give us the argument that certain information is very valuable to them and that they do not want their competitors to know about it. This is nonsense. The telephone books are full of the names of espionage agencies which will tell anyone the real worth of a company or person despite the credit ratings that are published and despite the financial statements.
There are many worth-while industrial espionage agencies which will give the financial standing as well as information concerning the habits, good and bad, of the directors of a company. Any information which would possibly be of value is open to scrutiny. If, indeed, information were secret, we would not have all these successful agencies which supply this information and make a good deal of money doing so. I do not believe there is a good argument that companies and corporations, private and public, which depend upon the law for certain protection should try to take advantage of another phase of the law by saying they do not have to give certain information. I can see no justification for that. I believe it is an argument concerning secrecy, and the argument that secrecy must be maintained because of competition is nonsense.
The minister has attempted to deal with the second phase of corporation law, that having to do with insider trading. This, of course, is one of the faults in our corporate structure. If we intend that our tax reform measures are to be successful, if we intend that our corporations are to grow and if we intend that the Canadian public should invest in shares of

these corporate structures, we must make sure the shareholders are given an even break. They are not given an even break today under the Canadian corporate structure. As has been pointed out by Professor John Porter in one case, and Mrs. Marjorie Keller recently, about 85 per cent of all our large corporations are controlled by a limited number of people, indeed 180 families at the moment. We have the tightest establishment in the world. Mind you, there is an establishment in Germany which is a family establishment. The Germans have a consaguinal family system which includes uncles, aunts, cousins and so on. If Mr. Krupp wanted to pass the business on to a member of the family, he had 413 heirs whom he considered to be family. Out of the 413 there would probably be one who would be able. In Canada, however, we think of the family as a conjugal matter and therefore consisting of sons and daughters. This limits us very much.
I have no particular quarrel with the establishment, provided it has ability and is fluid; but it is not. Our establishment does not depend on ability or success. Indeed, many members of the so-called elite-not so-called because it is actual-have not been successful. But they have been pure. Purity is the most important part of our establishment. You may never have a divorce. Once you have had one you are finished in the establishment. You may fail in business. I know one who has been bankrupt three times and is back in business. You must have a family which goes back at least 400 years. I recall discussing this matter. E. P. Taylor was never quite a member of the establishment because his father was a brewer. That was not far enough. You must go back at least four generations, and that makes you acceptable.
There is also an establishment in the United States, but it is fluid. If you are successful, you are in; if you are not successful, you are out. This is not the case in Canada. There is no new blood flowing into the corporate structures. This is what we are dealing with in respect of insider trading. The minister has tried to regulate this. There is an assumption that all transactions take place on the stock exchange. For instance, it is assumed that if I were to buy shares I would buy them there. But, no, control of shares is decided in clubs. It is not even polite to own your own shares. You say to Joe, a friend of yours, "You take about 7,000 of these shares and hold them for me and I will do the same for you." This is done in Toronto in three

Getting back to proxies, I think the proxy vote is one of the bad elements of our corporate structure. Anyone who has had anything to do with corporations as a shareholder will know that he will receive a proxy from the directors and be asked to sign it. In this way, he will allow someone else who will attend the meeting to vote for a certain director. What is not prohibited by the act, and what we do not all know, is that the present directors of the company, the people who now control the corporation, can send out proxies at the cost of the corporation. First of all, they know who the shareholders are and they have their addresses. They send out proxies at the company's expense, and it is almost certain that they will be re-elected because if a stranger to the board of directors disagreed with the choice of directors and wanted a new board of directors, first he would have to get the list of shareholders. This bill certainly improves the situation by providing only 20 days during which directors may be elected, and any shareholder can get a list of shareholders. This is a new provision.
If I wanted a new and efficient board of directors to be appointed, I would have to obtain the list of shareholders and at my own expense send them the proxies. My chances of getting the directors I wanted elected would not be good, whereas the existing board of directors can send the proxies out at the company's expense and it is certain that they will be re-elected.
Then, we have this fatherly distribution of directorships. Not long ago, a late senator gave 12 directorships to his son as a wedding present. It is difficult to comprehend how this can be done, but this is what happened in all likelihood. The senator said to a friend: "Look, my friend, my son, Jim, is getting married and I would like to do something for him. How about putting him on the board of your company?" His friend said: "All right. I have known Jim since he was knee high to a grasshopper". Of course, Jim has never been in the business, and in fact he had hardly been through law school, but on his wedding day he receives 12 directorships. That was a nice present.
A director does not receive a large salary because he only gets $500 a year. One wonders at the eagerness of people to become directors of companies, but there is a side benefit in being one. A director decides the time when the next distribution of shares will take place and who is to subscribe to them.

Someone has to write: "I, John Doe, will take
100,000	shares at $10 a share". He does not even have to invest a nickel because the shares are not yet issued. So, he puts down his name and has the right to get a certain number of shares as a director. Then, he can sell the rights to those shares. When the directors meet they ask whether everyone has disposed of the rights to their shares, and everyone agrees. The shares are then issued. So, although they have not invested a nickel, they make a lot of money for themselves. That is the great plum in being a director.
There is a good reason behind the U.S. law which requires that 50 per cent of the directors come from wilhin the corporation, that is people who make their living from the company. These are production managers, advertising managers and distribution vice-presidents. They are the people who make their living from the company and who want to make sure that the company functions. In our case only one man, the president, makes his bread and butter from the company, and 90 per cent of the directors are not at all interested in the corporate structure. Therefore, when we talk about proxies it would be a good idea for the minister-and I urge it upon him-to add a provision to the act that if the present directors or any shareholders send out proxies, they will be paid for by themselves. In the alternative, anyone who puts up a list of directors can send out proxies at the cost of the corporation. But you cannot have it both ways because it will not work. You will have a succession of the same directors over and over again and you will continue to have the same problem which exists today, that of an inefficient corporate structure.
In conclusion, I would like to congratulate the minister for presenting this bill. I think it is long overdue. I am sure he is aware of the failings of our corporate establishment, and I trust he will be able to continue to amend this act as quickly as possible in order to make our corporations workable and profitable, thus putting an end to the constant belittling of our corporate image. There is no reason for it. In this modern world we can only act under a corporate system, and if we keep lashing at our corporations because of faulty regulations, which are not their fault, we will not be doing our country any good. But if we word our regulations in such a way as not to give leeway to corporations to do something which Canadians believe should not be done, then we will solve the problem raised by an hon. member who said that
January 13. 1970

Canadians would rather put their money into U.S. investments than Canadian. I would do the same, and I would advise all hon. members to do so also because under the U.S. corporate structure shareholders are protected. They are assured that the best people direct the companies, that the Federal Securities Exchange Commission will protect their investment, and also that they do not have to depend on a limited number of self-perpetuating directors to run their companies.
If they invest in a Canadian company, they will be almost 100 per cent certain that it will be a family company using their money and that they will have absolutely no control over the conduct of that company.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) I think that the course which this debate has taken indicates that a much better method should have been adopted for dealing with this issue rather than the one that has been taken here. Obviously what the hon. member for York East and the hon. member for Timiskaming were saying, and to which there was agreement from at least one member, was that there were defects, that there had been irregularities, that there probably have been frauds and abuses of the corporate structure. It is essential, therefore, that there should be some means of dealing with this situation. But the divergence of opinion shows that in doing as he has done, the minister, together with his colleagues, the minor gods brooding on the top of Mount Olympus in the shadow of the major god, has handed down his divine judgment on just how we should deal with these problems. This way of acting has not made it possible for the House to discuss this matter thoroughly, and this is an essential condition for the passage of good legislation.
Surely, the legislative process might have been involved to bring about the appointment of a committee, with the fullest possible terms of reference, before the bill was actually introduced. Such a committee would have provided an opportunity for debate and discussion with people from all areas of our society who were involved and concerned in this matter, including the corporate people themselves and their representatives. So if it were established, as it should have been some time ago, this committee might have brought to the House and to the government its views, after a wide open discussion and national debate which I think is essential, and recom-
Canada Corporations Act mended the terms of a statute. I think this is a procedure which could be adopted far more often. We hear a lot of rumblings today about the parliamentary system, its value and benefit. In my humble opinion, we do not seek the opportunity to make the best use of this system, and I think this is a typical illustration.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It might well be that in such a committee we would find divergencies. I might find myself parting company with the hon. member for York East in certain of his views, although he seems to have an adequate knowledge of the corporate structure. I might find myself in distinct opposition to the hon. member for Timiskaming. However, the public would have had an opportunity to peer through the plate glass window-of Parliament and watch the formulation of proposals. The whole parliamentary system would have been involved.
The minister, anticipating objection to this particular measure in the form it has taken, has attempted, in the way that honourable and learned members who belong to the same profession as he and I, to rebut anticipated objections. At page 706 of Hansard, in the course of a lengthy preliminary statement, the minister is reported as follows:
I can hardly believe that in this day and age they-
And, here he means people who would object to the proposals
-want the government of the land to stand beyond the reach of the criticism of the citizens: that they want to allow the government of the land to take decisions that affect us all on the basis of information not available to the public.
The minister may correct me, but it seems to me he has the opportunity to have the last say, at least at this stage of the proceedings. He may assert that there are other statements in his speech which go beyond that but I think that here he is anticipating the objections which may be taken. I submit that this is a weak, insipid and illogical basis on which to rest legislation which gives such great authority to this government.
If the minister were to some extent honest about this he would admit that he is a young and ambitious minister. I have nothing against youth and ambition. I only wish I could have youth back without arrbition! The minister and his ambitious departmental establishment seek to add to their already substantial power. He is a member of a gov-

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act ernment which has already obtained great authority and which seeks to make itself an even more powerful government. This bill, together with several companion measures dealing with financial institutions, indicate the power the government seeks. The Investment Companies Act, which is still to come forward, was taken to pieces in the other place the last time it was presented. According to my information, the government intends to bring it back, basically in its original form,-I cannot accept the minister shaking his head at this time-in the belief that having passed it through this House, the senate will be compelled to accept it as a bill which has been passed by this body.
In my opinion, these measures all form part of a rather devious scheme of the government which would potentially have the effect of intimidating corporations both large and small, compelling them to fall in line with whatever the government may wish from time to time.
Let me make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that there is no doubt, as I said before, that there is ample room, ample need and a requirement for the improvement of the corporations Act and many of the other statutes which govern the incorporation and operation of other corporate bodies under federal jurisdiction.
But the over-all effect of this bill is to place in the hands of a government of partisan politicians authoritarian rights which I am convinced can be and will be exercised from time to time for political purposes. Of course, there have been instances in the past of improprieties and wrongs committed which resulted in losses to individual shareholders and I suppose this will happen again. There has been fraud, inadequate information and failure to take action at the appropriate time to prevent such losses. But I submit that it would be possible to cure these instances of company iniquity by other means, and it was not essential for this government to seize to itself the powers they have sought to swell themselves up to the proportions of Big Brother, peering, poking or threatening to do the things I have mentioned.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and others have talked solemnly about the right to privacy. What a farce this contention is now revealed to be in the light of the various corporate statutes which this government is seeking to have amended at this session. What we have is big government becoming

ever bigger, with more employees, more bureaucracy and the everswelling establishment.
As I sit back and watch the operations of this government I can only say, "God help the poor individual". There will be liitle place left for him in our society by the time the present administration is finished with its various proposals. In every session we find more and more of the rights and freedoms of individuals being circumscribed. It would be bad enough even if this were a government which was doing something to bring about the just society, what my friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) would probably call the red herring which was dangled before some of the electors of Canada. The situation would be bad enough, even if it were a government trying to do something about the ever-increasing problems of rapid urbanization and all its ancillary problems, a government really making some substantial effort to tackle the environmental problem of pollution and all the other problems and difficulties facing our society today. Even if it were trying to do something, making some effort, I would still be unhappy. But I am even more concerned about giving these powers to a government which is doing nothing. I say that we are in danger of giving a great deal more power to a government which obviously seeks to exercise that power for the sake of power alone.
In proof of this, Mr. Speaker, I could list some of the bills which are on the order paper. If they were relative I could quote the clauses in the bills which the government has cited as part of their legislative fare for this session. However, it would take too much time and in any event I would probably be out of order. I shall reserve that pleasure for another day, Mr. Speaker.
At page 709 of Hansard, in a speech dealing with a question of the investigative rights being taken by the government or at least by an emanation of the government, the minister says that since 1950 the department has received only 11 formal requests for inspection. In other words, there have been only 11 requests for inspection over a period of 20 years. The minister went on to say that there had been a number of informal complaints but he did not indicate whether these informal complaints had any substance to them and ended up by saying, "that the inspection was useful in showing that suspicions of irregularities or misconduct were groundless and baseless."
January 13, 1970

For some reason or other, Mr. Speaker, despite what the minister mentions in his own speech, there is obviously a very limited need for the kind of investigative opportunity he seeks to obtain. Nevertheless, the procedures must be altered to allow the minister and other government people almost unlimited opportunities for these fishing expeditions.
In my view there is no doubt that the proposals would give the government an opportunity to harass and destroy corporations which might have angered or annoyed the government, a government of partisan politicians. This is a situation we should be very careful about, particularly in the light of the record of this particular administration.
My hon. colleague from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has dealt with a number of provisions of the legislation. I want to limit my specific discussion now to clause 11 which gives almost unlimited power and right of investigation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The Financial Times is certainly not a periodical which can be said to be unfriendly to this government, but they have taken a look at this situation. In the editions of November 10, 17 and 24 there are statements and editorials which bear clearly and succinctly on the point I am making. My friends on the other side of the House and others may say that this particular publication speaks for business. Probably it does, but there is nothing wrong in having a publication which speaks for businessmen. Most of us are, or at some time have been, in business. Most people are in some form of business and many who are not would like to be in business-except if they have read the white paper on taxation. Merely because a man is a businessman that does not mean that he is free from the bad habits to which other individuals may be subject. There are defects in societies as well as in individuals, and corporations are composed of businessmen who are individuals. Those individuals are all subject to the frailties of human nature. When those individuals are combined together, their combined frailties can sometimes create more danger and havoc than would be possible for any ordinary individual.
I do not think we should assume that merely because a person is carrying on a business or merely because a corporation is carrying on a business, that that person or corporation is thereby to be condemned automatically and subjected to unwarranted
Canada Corporations Act and unjustified investigation and interference. That should not be permitted unless a prima facie case can be made.
May I now read from the editorial of the Financial Times of November 10, which reads in part:
The federal government's bill to revise The Canada Corporations Act has been lying around since last May and will soon be coming up for examination by a committee of the House of Commons. It needs a drastic overhaul. In its present form it is intolerable not only to business but to every Canadian with a concern for civil liberties....
Some of the most objectionable proposals are outlined in the report on page 3, and we hope they will be widely studied. Many of them can be met with quite simple amendments, but there are two fundamental flaws in the draft sponsored by Mr. Basford as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The first is the almost unrestricted power Mr. Basford wants for himself and the bureaucrats of the combines branch who report to him. Without any outside check beyond the approval of the government-appointed Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, Mr. Basford (or any ambitious politician who may succeed him) is authorized to 'investigate' any company whom he may choose to suspect of doing something wrong or damaging the interest of even one shareholder.
'To investigate' means to provide a team of bureaucrats with legal sanction to enter any premises, seize, examine and copy any documents it wants; examine any witnesses it likes under oath; search, prod and probe as long as it wishes for anything it may hope to discover______
To give such powers as this to a minister and his bureaucracy smacks of a totalitarian regime, not a democracy. In the hands of an unscrupulous government they could be used to threaten, harass or destroy any company which happened to incur a minister's displeasure. It is unthinkable that Parliament should accept them in their present form.
The second thing basically wrong with Mr. Bas-ford's bill is that it virtually invites any shareholder to harass and disrupt any company at the expense of all the other shareholders without risk to himself. It is a charter of irresponsibility for every nut and crank who enjoys making a nuisance of himself....
The federal bill seems to have been drafted on the assumption that every unhappy shareholder is being victimized and that every company director is a criminal. It ain't necessarily so. And the danger of the assumption is that honest men will be deterred from becoming directors rather than face so many almost impossible duties under the threat of going to jail.
The Corporations Act needs revising. The purpose behind the revision is right. But the end can never justify the means Mr. Basford is proposing.
A good case can be made for allowing a powerful investigative function to be exercised, not by government, but by the courts or a division of the courts with jurisdiction to

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act deal with problems of this kind. I know that the courts are also subject to the frailties of human nature. But the judicial process is still sound and there is a court of appeal. With the introduction of provisions involving a limitation on costs it may be possible for those who have legitimate grievances to have these matters examined. I do not think it is beyond the ingenuity of the minister and his officials to draft proposals which are acceptable, so that real and potential irregularities which may occur will be subject to examination. That examination should not be conducted under the provisions of this bill; neither should this government be given the powers it is seeking in the bill. My remarks would apply to any government, but particularly to this one.

Will the hon. member permit a question. The editorial the hon. member read stated, I think, that civil liberties are being denied to corporations, or will be denied if this bill passes. Does the hon. member support the theory that a corporation is entitled to civil liberties, or does he say that individuals only are entitled to civil liberties?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, clearly, in the first instance, the answer is that a corporation is composed of individuals. I meant to make that point clear. I do not deny that there is a right to investigate, but I object to the way the government is proposing to do it. We should not put so much power into the hands of government and government officials. That is my primary objection. There is a good case no doubt for relief and reform, but I object to the end result the passage of this bill will entail. Perhaps this government will be replaced by another, who knows. Who knows what the situation in this respect may be in the next year or the next decade. All too often we have seen the tragic example of governments saying to their people, "We are only adopting these powers in theory; we may never use them, and we will certainly never abuse them."
All too often we find that governments break their promises. At the same time I say that if more care and thought had been exercised, and proper attention paid to due processes of law, it would have been possible for the government to bring in appropriate amendments. I agree with hon. members who have spoken before; we could have had a completely new corporations act. That could have been the subject of examination by committee. The Committee could start ab initio, bring forward proposals for legislation based on needs, requirements, knowledge and

experiences of the past, and thereby introduce a bill which would deal with the problems which have been mentioned. In such new bill I think it might be possible to devise a simple and inexpensive procedure to bring these matters before the judiciary. It might be possible to have investigations conducted by independent bodies which would work completely outside the ambit of government interference. It could be a quasi-judicial body. In any event, I do not like the powers suggested in the bill to be in the hands of a minister or at the disposal of a government.
It has become apparent in the last year or two that a significant characteristic of this government is that it seeks to take unto itself powers which should be exercised by bodies such as the courts, which have an independence which is absolutely essential if we are to secure the free, independent and non-political evaluation of certain matters. Such an evaluation is required in order to preserve a proper balance in our society where we have the mixture of the executive, legislative and judicial functions.
If, on the other hand, it appears that the courts might not have the capacity, either because of lack of facilities or overloads of work, to make these inquiries and investigations, I think it would have been preferable if we had established tribunals which would have the same degree of independence as the courts. The members of these tribunals would have the same amount of freedom as is exercised by the judiciary-freedom resulting from the terms of their appointment and tenure of office.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In saying this, I am by no means downgrading the effectiveness and the usefulness of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. I think these people do a very fine job, particularly having in mind the limited nature of the terms of reference given to them under the constitutional limitation which, to some extent, plagues the federal administration.
I repeat that I am becoming more and more alarmed at the trend of the government of the right hon. gentleman and his friends to arrogate to themselves, to take into their own hands, the strength and the power to unduly dominate our society. The whole thing smacks too much of a star-chamber procedure. The bill provides that there can be an ex-parte power given to direct an investigation.
The inspectors are appointed ex-parte and the order for the examination of a person is
January 13, 1970

made ex-parte. A person being examined is not, as of right, entitled to counsel, as I understand the bill. In any case, counsel would not be of much assistance since the powers granted to the Commission are so broad that a witness cannot refuse to answer any question, even if it might tend to incriminate him. This is a power which our courts are loathe to grant to the prosecution, even in criminal cases of the most serious nature. An inspector appointed by the commissioner is granted the widest conceivable powers of search. It is incredible that in a country where the rule of law is supposedly respected such an inquisition should be permitted. If such powers were granted to magistrates under the Criminal Code there would be an immediate outcry, even if such powers were used for the purpose of detecting the commission of extremely serious criminal offences.
I call attention to proposed section 112D which provides for the payment of the cost of investigation. It is surely against the principles of natural justice that in all circumstances a person should pay for the investigation of his own affairs in preparation for possible prosecution, whether or not he is convicted of an offence at a later date. What about the possibility of the power being used for improper purposes? Some individual or group might propose that an investigation be held. Having conducted the investigation it might then be found there was no need at all for the investigation and, as a matter of fact, it was brought about only for the purpose of harassment. Surely, under such circumstances, provision should be made and the cost of such an investigation should be paid by the instigator. This would include the Crown. This, of course, shows the one-sided nature of this type of investigation when such power is placed in the hands of this government.
In my view, it would have been much more practical to have appointed an all-party committee of this House with the widest possible terms of reference, with power to inquire fully into this problem and propose legislation after having given an opportunity for all interested persons to appear and make their point of view known.

Mr. Speaker, John Kenneth Galbraith in his book "The New Industrial State" points out that since the turn of the century North American business has moved steadily from being an accretion of small business enterprise to the development of large and
Canada Corporations Act powerful corporations. He points out that these corporations have now become multinational in scope and that they have developed what are commonly called conglomerates that have moved into different fields of industry. They have established vertical integration. They control a product from its raw state right through to the marketing and, in some cases, the retailing of the product.
He points out that many of these gigantic corporations have incomes which exceed the budgets of some smaller nations, that they control their source of supply, that they are able to generate their own capital; they are able to virtually set their own prices and by vast advertising campaigns to largely control the buying patterns of the public. In his book Galbraith establishes the fact that on the North American continent we have now developed what he calls a corporate oligopoly with a huge technostructure that has a life of its own and that is virtually a state within a state.
He quite properly points out that in spite of all the indignation that may be generated about this development, no one in their right senses thinks that we can ever go back to the small businessman and the free enterprise economy of the nineteenth century. With mass production techniques and industrial rationalization, with a large pool of trained manpower and the research which is essential for modern industry, these gigantic corporations will continue to operate and it is needless to talk about breaking them up, as was talked about many years ago in the United States when the Sherman anti-trust laws and other legislation was passed. We must now devote our attention to ensuring that these large corporate bodies are made responsible to the public interest in one form or another. That certainly ought to be the purpose of the legislation which is now before the House.
I understand it is some 34 years since this Corporations Act was amended to any great degree. I think it is a great pity that when it does come before the House it is not going to cover a wider scope than is envisaged in the bill. The bill does propose some steps which will certainly improve the situation.
The point I want to make this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is that a Corporations Act ought to do more than concern itself with mere corporation housekeeping. It ought to be concerned with more than merely providing for increased information and increased protection for the investor. This legislation ought also to concern itself with protecting Canada's

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act national sovereignty and with diminishing the increased takeover of the Canadian economy by foreign investors. It is serious enough when a country is controlled by a corporate elite, that is a negation of true democracy, but when a country is controlled by a corporate elite outside its own borders, its capacity to resolve the situation is tremendously reduced. No country is truly free when the development of its economy is controlled by foreign investment. Our political democracy is curtailed when a corporate elite controls the economy of our nation. But when a foreign corporate elite has a nation in its grip we have lost any chance of building genuine social democracy and even political democracy itself is in jeopardy.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We in the New Democratic Party believe that the issue of Canadian economic and political independence is now and will continue to be the central issue of this decade. We do not think this issue can be evaded much longer. The constant drift to continentalism of past and present Liberal governments threatens to paralyze our efforts to establish a distinctive national identity in Canada. The escalating foreign control and take-over of our economy has reached alarming proportions and continues virtually unimpeded. As a result, Canada's options for the future are being increasingly closed off.
The Liberal government itself recognized this growing menace to Canadian independence. This is why under the administration of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson they set up a royal commission which has come to be called the Watkins Commission. That commission, consisting of some of the ablest economists in Canada, brought in its report. I shall not take the time of the House by going over the various recommendations; some of my hon. friends may do so in the course of the debate. The interesting thing is that although this report has been in the hands of the government for several years, and though it has been discussed in the press all over the country, no statement has yet been made by the government as to what it proposes to do about the recommendations-which of them it considers impracticable and which of them it considers acceptable and deserving of implementation. No statement at all has been forthcoming.
In the meantime, the situation which caused the commission to be set up has grown immeasurably more serious. The Watkins [Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
Commission pointed out that Canada was the only country in the world which allowed so much of its economy to be owned by investors outside its borders. It pointed out that some two-thirds of our economy was under foreign control. Since that time the rate of takeover has accelerated in an alarming way. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) tabled an answer to a question by my hon. friend the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) a short time ago showing that since 1963 some 606 corporations coming under federal jurisdiction had been bought out by foreign corporations. This is to say nothing, of course, of the hundreds of companies coming under provincial jurisdiction which have also been bought out. Many of them are major companies, long established firms which have done business in Canada and which have now been brought under the direct control of foreign corporations.
The Watkins Commission pointed out that no other industrialized nation in the world has permitted such blatant takeovers of its economy as did Canada. Nearly all the industrialized nations have imposed restrictions upon economic takeovers. Most of the countries of Europe, Great Britain and the United States itself, have imposed restrictions, in some cases severe in nature. Japan, a country which has received a great deal of United States investment since the end of the second world war, passed legislation two years ago restricting foreign investment in any industry to 49 per cent and in the case of certain key industries such as transportation and steel production, to 20 per cent. In banking, finance and the communications media no foreign investment at all is permitted.
I would point out to those who get nervous when we discuss this subject in case we might frighten off United States capital, that the Americans, who have tremendous investments in Japan, did not pack up their bags and go home. They accepted the situation, recognizing that the Japanese were justified in drawing the line and saying they could not allow their entire economy and the decisionmaking power of the nation to be vested in people from another country.
The Canadian government has taken no such action. We took action on the question of the banks only after one bank had been taken over. We took no action with respect to finance companies until Merrill, Lynch and Associates took over Royal Securities. We have taken no other action with respect to the
January 13, 1970

acquisition of Canadian corporations by foreign investors. The Canadian government has done nothing, either because it has been cowed into submission or because it is convinced that economic absorption is inevitable. Whether the reason is cowardice or indifference I suggest the result is the same; the result is that in Canada we shall lose not only the control of our economy but eventually even the control of our decision-making power unless we stop this steady erosion of our sovereignty, this diminution of our independence.
If history teaches us anything at all, Mr. Speaker, it is that political control always follows economic control. We had an example of this not many years ago. We know that legislation was introduced by a Liberal government to make two United States periodicals, Time and Reader's Digest, virtually and legally Canadian corporations in order that they might get the benefits of being Canadian publications. The Minister of Finance at that time, Mr. Walter Gordon, has since stated publicly that pressure was brought to bear upon him and upon the government by the government in Washington which had obligations to Mr. Henry Luce and to other powerful figures in the United States. Economic control always lays the basis for political control. Once a country loses its power to make economic decisions, increasingly it loses its power to make decisions with respect to an independent foreign policy, with respect to developing its own culture and with respect to establishing its own national identity.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
One of the latest signs of this which gives us concern is the talk about integration of resources in North America. I should like to refer to a meeting held in Washington by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and Mr. Walter Hickel, Secretary of the Interior of the United States. At this meeting preliminary discussions were held with regard to an integrated energy policy for North America, and in this connection I should like to quote a report in the December 5 edition of the Globe and Mail of the press conference that the minister held in Washington:
Asked whether this approach would lead to a substantial economic integration of the two countries, Mr. Greene replied: "Yes, X think it would."
The minister went on to say:
If Canada had refused any economic integration with the United States for nationalist reasons, it would be no more than "a banana republic."
Canada Corporations Act
The minister must have got his facts back to front, because it is the banana republics that are the very ones that have succumbed to complete economic control and domination by outside investors. If we in this country succumb to the same kind of domination, although we may be a little more sophisticated and better off than some of the South America banana republics, the fact remains that we will become an economic colony of the United States.

There is no argument about that, Mr. Speaker; it seems to be agreed on both sides of the House. This is why we are worried about the question.
Then the minister, according to the report, went on to say:
It Is "sufficient" for Canada to retain political control. It is not important who gets the dividends, Wall Street or Bay Street-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
That is right.
Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands: The minister says that is right. I want to point out that it makes a great deal of difference who gets the dividends. First of all, if the dividends are paid on Bay Street, they are taxable in Canada. The companies are subject to Canadian law and to Canadian control. They are subject to the policies of the government of Canada. On the other hand, foreign investors have taken the position that they are not subject to Canadian law but to the law of the United States or whatever country within which the parent company is located.
Much more important than that, the corporation that owns an operation in Canada has decision making power. For example, it has the power to decide whether certain materials will be developed now, or left in the ground for 25 or 50 years while the company uses up resources it owns in other parts of the world; whether our natural resources will be shipped out of the country in their raw state, providing Canada with minimal employment, or whether they will be processed here, thus developing the Canadian economy and providing employment for Canadian workers; whether the price charged the parent company will return a profit to Canada and pay taxes to Canada, or whether Canadian raw

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act material will be sold to the parent company-in the United States at a price that realizes virtually no profit to Canada, thus depriving the Canadian government of revenue. That is the type of decision making power we are giving away as well as giving away control of our resources.
The fact of the matter is that the United States has been, and is, using our resources to expand its industry. From the point of view of the U.S. this is, of course, a perfectly proper thing to do. The United States has developed the greatest industrial complex in the world and requires more and more raw materials and more and more sources of energy. The closest source of those materials required to meet the needs of the expanding economy of the United States is Canada.
So, it is natural that the United States wants an integrated policy that will supply particularly those resources which are in short supply or almost entirely depleted. What this Parliament has to be concerned about, and particularly the minister who is piloting through this legislation, is whether or not our resources are going to be used first and foremost to develop and expand the Canadian economy, to provide jobs for Canadian workers and to raise the standard of living of the Canadian people, we being able to export the surplus commodities that we do not require. Such decision making power does not lie here in Ottawa on the treasury benches; more and more it is being delegated to the boardrooms of large corporations that are not located within the borders of Canada.

that Bill C-13, to establish the office of parliamentary commissioner, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-13 is one that I have had the privilege of presenting to the House for the last seven years. It would establish in this country at the federal level the office of ombudsman. Unfortunately, the Liberal party, which has been responsible for forming past governments, has not decided to institute such an office, in spite of the fact that four years ago a parliamentary committee that studied this bill in depth unanimously recommended to the House that a parliamentary commissioner be appointed.
In the Speech from the Throne in the 1965 session, it was stated that the government would establish an ombudsman during that session. Yet the government saw fit to take no action. Many times I asked the previous Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, as well as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when the government intended to go ahead and establish such an essential office. The most recent reply was that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) could very well be the ombudsman for Canada. The Minister of Justice is a very fine gentleman. I think a great deal of him and know he is very efficient and able, but it just seems to me that he has not a hope in the world of ever serving the people of his country as ombudsman. I do not say that against him personally, but because the very nature of his office makes this impossible.

Let me cite an example of my experience during my years in this house. This concerns the Department of Veterans Affairs. During session after session I have had veterans of our armed forces bring legitimate gripes and complaints as they relate pension treatment to my attention. I had one just a few weeks ago which concerned a man who applied for his release, I believe in the month

Mr. Justice Milvain ruled in favour of the ombudsman. This ruling, given just a few days ago, is very significant.

He has often said to me that one of the greatest benefits of his office is derived not so much from the fact that he investigates and recommends to the government and its various departments, but from the fact that he is there. This has a salutary effect upon government officials who tend to forget about individual needs. They are dealing with rulings and regulations and tend to look at cases from a legal point of view rather than from moral responsibility. The fact that an ombudsman is present has a very wholesome effect on the attitude of senior civil servants. On the other hand, it has a very wholesome effect on the general population because people who feel the government is injust in its tax policies or various decisions that affect them know they have a man to whom they can appeal without spending $30,000 on an appeal to the Exchequer Court, for example, or without having to go to the courts when they feel they cannot afford to or when it would not really be worth the effort.
Sir Guy Powles has said publicly in his report, and I believe Mr. McClellan has reaffirmed this on several occasions, that one of the greatest advantages of the office of ombudsman or, as we call it in this bill, a parliamentary commissioner, is the fact that he is there. This is good for the populace and is good for senior civil servants. Incidentally, I think it is very helpful to the ministers of the crown. Perhaps the Minister of Justice would find himself free of many petty things he has to deal with which consume his time and perhaps prevent him from devoting his attention to things that would seem to be more important.

Thus, speaking now to the members of this House, I hope that tonight we can give second reading to this bill and refer it to the committee. Then, the Committee could hear the evidence that has been gathered since it last considered this bill favourably, evidence relating to the established practice and use of this office in the provinces.

The Auditor General, of necessity, finds himself dealing with cases which ought to belong to the office of an ombudsman. I am grateful he is there and I am glad he does this.
And they cut his staff.

I do not understand why they cut his staff. If the office of an ombudsman is not to be established, they ought to expand his staff so that at least in the areas of taxation and financial administration the people of Canada might have some recourse.
I would commend this bill to the members of this House and to the Minister of Justice. I hope the government will do something about it.

us. This is an educational process. It gives me the opportunity to express some views on the concept of this avenue of remedy against administrative decisions in a modern complicated government. The hon. member did not go so far as to define what he meant by ombudsman.
We have talked about it many times.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I understand it, what he is talking about is an independent person, one independent of the
January 13, 1970

executive and independent of the legislature but one who reports to the legislature.
Responsible to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Responsible to parliament and given authority and certain statutory powers to investigate matters of governmental administration, in this case federal administration, which give rise to individual grievances on the part of the citizens of this country. In other words, his terms of reference would be to review the administration or more particularly mal-administra-tion within the ranks of the federal public service.
At the outset I want to concede that one of the threats to individual well-being in Canada is the dwarfing of individual rights compared to the growing complexity and strength of government, whether it be at the federal or provincial level. One of the thrusts, as I have tried to state before, of the Department of Justice is to seek ways to balance the rights of the individual Canadian against his government. As the hon. member said, we are faced with a situation where government has become more remote from the average Canadian. Government has become larger, more complex, more bureaucratic and perhaps more arbitrary. Certainly, it has become less sensitive. I believe it is incumbent upon this House to review continually the avenues of appeal, of redress and of remedy against arbitrariness in the governmental structure.
I am personally very concerned about the motivation behind the hon. member's bill. I was in the United Kingdom last October where I had discussions with the law officers of the Crown, the members of the Law Reform Commission that they have in England and Wales and the members of the Scottish Law Reform Commission. I took the opportunity at that time to go to Sweden where I met the Swedish ombudsman, Alfred Bexelius, on October 2. I spent four hours with him that morning. I had lunch with him and was able to return his hospitality by inviting him to dinner. As a matter of fact, I told him he was one of the famous men of the world representing what had become a very celebrated institution. I told him that the word "ombudsman" had become as familiar to people outside Sweden as the word "smorgasbord" and that the institution which he fills and which dates back to 1809 when the new constitution of Sweden was first written was something all modern governments were looking to for guidance.

As a matter of fact, there are now three ombudsmen with equal jurisdiction in Sweden because the work available for a single ombudsman has gone beyond what he was able to handle personally. When I returned to London I spent two hours with Sir Edmund Compton, the parliamentary commissioner who is responsible to the Parliament of the United Kingdom. His office has been established since 1967. I had the opportunity to discuss the institution and efficacy of the ombudsman with the attorney general of England, with the Lord Chancellor, the Solicitor General and a good many members of Parliament. I inquired of them what their views were of the institution and how it was working within a parliamentary system based upon the British tradition.
I am quite aware that the institution has become contagious. We have in Canada three provinces which now have their own ombudsman. The hon. member for Red Deer represents Alberta and he will know that Alberta is represented by Mr. McClellan, formerly the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. New Brunswick has an ombudsman and last year the province of Quebec established the office of Protecteur du Peuple, the citizens' protector. Now, we have three ombudsmen at the provincial level. There are ombudsmen not only in Sweden but also in the other Scandinavian countries, Denmark and Finland, as well as in New Zealand and now in Hawaii.
Might I just remind the minister that the province of Manitoba passed legislation in this regard but the appointment has not yet been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I am half right and half wrong.
May I suggest in the comments I am going to make that there is some difficulty in accepting the precedents of other jurisdictions and that Parliament here in Ottawa ought to scrutinize the traditions under which these offices have been established in other jurisdictions to see whether they apply with equal force to Canada. In Sweden the ombudsman has almost complete jurisdiction to investigate administrative discretion. There are virtually no limits on his authority. He can review any aspect of governmental administration in the country, including military administration, ecclesiastical administration and the courts. But there are certain aspects of government in Sweden which differ substantially from our own. More importantly
2326	COMMONS
Provision for Parliamentary Commissioner there is no ministerial responsibility as we know it in Canada. The ministers of the Crown in Sweden are not responsible before the legislature for the acts or omissions of their departmental officials.
The public service in Sweden is not governed by a system of subordinate responsibility whereby a man in a lower position automatically is responsible to his superior and so on through the deputy minister to a minister, but is governed instead by statutes and laws and is responsible only to themselves on the basis of the interpretation of their powers as found in the statutes and regulations.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
There being no ministerial responsibility, there is no way in which the people of Sweden can challenge maladministration on the floor of their parliament. Secondly, and this is a fundamental difference, the Swedish member of Parliament has no fundamental right to voice a grievance on behalf of his constituent or of any citizen of Sweden. He cannot challenge on the floor of his Parliament a factual situation relating to a particular grievance; he is limited to challenging the principles of the law governing that situation.
I might also suggest to the House that when we are talking about the Scandinavian countries, New Zealand and the other jurisdictions that have adopted the ombudsman idea, we are dealing with small, relatively homogenous populations. As a matter of fact, those members of the House who have had the opportunity to visit Sweden know that the Swedes are such a homegenous race that they need not speak to each other. They can sit silently over a meal, say nothing, and yet instinctively know what the other thinks.
The only country of any sizeable complexity and sizeable population that has adopted the idea-

He has no jurisdiction over local government. I am suggesting to you that in the only country with any sizeable population in which that institution has been adopted extreme limitations have been put on the jurisdiction of that commissioner.
Another difficulty-I am trying to point these out as best I can-is that we are living in a federal state with a divided jurisdiction and shared responsibilities among federal and provincial governments. I will not be the first to point out that a good many of the complaints that would inevitably reach the office of any federal ombudsman would involve matters not within the federal jurisdiction but falling under the authority of the provinces and the municipalities. My friend, the hon. member for Red Deer, knows as well as I do that most Canadians really do not know whether a matter is a local one to be dealt with by municipal or town authorities or a matter involving the province or the federal government.
That is no argument at all.

I am suggesting also that in a large geographical and territorial area like Canada it would be difficult-and I think we have to anticipate this-for any federal ombudsman to be able to see the complainant personally, review the file and render his decision. I have had a chat with Mr. McClelland, Alberta's ombudsman, and he tells me that it is essential that the

volume of work never exceed what the ombudsman personally can review, that he should not operate with more than a small staff. That was echoed by the other gentlemen to whom I talked. The reason is that unless the ombudsman is personally able to review the file, and if necessary personally able to interview the complainant, then all he establishes is a second bureaucracy superimposed on the first. This is something that in a federal state, particularly a federal state with a large geographical area, we would have to be concerned with in Canada.
I also have some concern about what appeal there would be from an ombudsman's decision. The very concept of that office gives a lot of discretion, jurisdiction and omnipotence to a single man. There is no appeal from him. In the event that an ombudsman would render an adverse judgment against a citizen, to my mind any further avenue of redress would virtually be foreclosed. I remember that during the discussion of the powers of the official languages commissioner, whose powers are very similar to those of the ombudsman in Alberta, concern was expressed on the other side of the House about the powers given to the commissioner and about the fact that there was no right of appeal. Our reply was that this was not a judicial office or judicial proceeding-nor is the ombudsman-and that the commissioner's only power was the power of publicity and the power to bring the grievance to public notice and to the notice of parliament. I recall that at that time hon. members were concerned that there were no methods of appealing the commissioner's decision.
Let me look now at what the government is doing to try to remedy the situation for which the hon. member has suggested the institution of an ombudsman, what we are trying to do both by way of parliamentary redress and by way of judicial review to enhance the rights of the individual citizen against administrative decisions. First of all, we are committed to the establishment of a federal law reform commission, and I hope to be able to submit to the scrutiny of Parliament a draft of that bill in first reading within the next month. That reform commission will be charged with the review of the general terms of the criminal law and of the substantive administrative public law of this country. The throne speech also commits the government to a wide area of administrative law reform. We intend to set up a wider system of judicial review by the courts of all decisions of federal administrative boards and federal administrative

His argument is persuasive. I have had the advantage of conversations with Sir Edmund Compton and Mr. Alfred Bexelius. I admit that one of the advantages of an ombudsman is the very fact of his presence-the fact that he is there. In gaining a reputation as the people's protector, he becomes a psychological barrier to arbitrariness; he is a safety valve. People have the idea that there is someone to whom they can turn.
I believe we can succeed in improving the scrutiny of Parliament, in enhancing the role of the individual Member of Parliament in his ability to bring a grievance of the people before this chamber, in controlling the scope of the enabling power to make regulations and in widening the legal remedies of the citizen. If we find that those wider parliamentary powers of the legislature as against the executive, and thereby the administration- wider judicial powers of the citizen against

administrative tribunals-fail to do that, I admit there is a case for an extralegal and extraparliamentary remedy along the lines of an ombudsman.
I want to warn the House that procedural safeguards-and this is a type of procedural safeguard from which there is no appeal, the only remedy being publicity and report to Parliament-cannot substitute for an improvement in the scrutiny of Parliament and an improvement in our public administrative law.
Chief Justice McRuer, in the fourth volume of the second report of his monumental study of civil rights in Ontario at page 1389, says that he is not convinced that the ombudsman is one of the most urgent needs in the process of democratic government in Ontario. He had a conversation with Sir Guy Powles, the New Zealand ombudsman, who says the ombudsman is not the complete answer to all the problems of the administration of justice.
This government is going to do its best to widen the scope of parliamentary and judicial review. We are going to do our best through a broadening of the committee system, through a broadening of the avenues of grievance available to the individual Member of Parliament-who, after all, is the fundamental protector of the people of Canada-to achieve what the hon. member wants achieved. Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief, but I feel it is my duty to support Bill C-13, sponsored by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), and entitled: "An Act to establish the Office of Parliamentary Commissioner".
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have given my place to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner); this has enabled me to get to know his arguments concerning Bill C-13.
I am surprised to note that the Minister of Justice whom I have always regarded as the protector of public rights, as the defender of citizens' rights and as the promoter of justice and equity even on behalf of the most humble people has not given his opinion on this bill while using the time allotted to him. In fact, he has told us in details of his trip to England and to other countries, thus proving to us that the trips he is making are more serious than those of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

However, that does not tell us whether the minister agrees with the principle of Bill C-13. His arguments seem to me very weak and this leads me to believe that the bill in itself is perhaps not so bad.
Among other things, I recall an argument put forth by the minister and that surprised me, coming from a man that I have always held in high esteem. He said that the function of parliamentary commissioner might not be as necessary and desirable as might be expected at the federal level, because we have, in Canada, a federal system. True, there are ten provinces, with different needs, concepts and objectives, and the federal goven-ment has its own jurisdiction, in accordance with the British North America Act.
The minister said that the office of parliamentary commissioner is not as necessary and desirable as it is claimed for the simple reason that the citizens do not know from whom they must seek information and that the role of this parliamentary commissioner would only be to tell them. Now, even if the parliamentary commissioner's only role were to tell the citizens where to apply to solve their problems it would be a marked and obvious improvement on the present situation.
Besides, without playing politics, I would like to tell the minister that whether they are on the government side or in the opposition all hon. members are now considered by the citizens as social workers. In fact, people come to us and ask that we help them and represent them not only in the House, which is part of our functions, but also with the civil servants of various departments.

They cannot be blamed for it. In fact, governments have never actually enlightened the population in this regard. Moreover, the governmental administration is constantly expanding. It has become a mammoth that can only be stirred with great difficulty in order to draw from it equity, justice and humanity.

I remember a recent television interview with the Ombudsman of Quebec. This telecast was very instructive for me because it gave me the opportunity to realize the important role such a commissioner could play at a time where the administration of our governments gets more and more complicated.
Mr. Speaker, the argumentation of the minister is inconsistent and has nothing to do with the true situation in Canada. It is precisely because the jurisdictional fields of the various governments are increasingly overlapping that people no longer know where to go, even members of parliament. If we consider the problem of social security, economic expansion, agriculture, transportation or justice, we note that the departments are overlapping at all levels of government.

He can appeal a criminal or civil case to a superior court, but he cannot appeal the decision of an official. Even if the minister told me that it can be done, he knows quite well that due to the complexity of the administration and to the fact that officials generally only perform bureaucratic work and very often unfortunately forget the human aspect, it would be difficult to obtain justice.
