A University of Ottawa professor, Mr. Raoul P. Barbe, whom the minister probably knows, recently published a manual of administrative law which is the work of a team. An expert whose political neutrality is above any suspicion says clearly that federal and provincial administrations should tend increasingly to get closer to the people under their jurisdiction. It is also said that the relationships between those who govern and those who are governed should gain in justice and fairness.

Mr. Speaker, because I should like to see this bill referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, where it can be studied much more thoroughly, I shall speak for only a few minutes. In any case, I find it is not necessary to speak at greater length; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) knows our thoughts, after his sojourn in Sweden, and it is good to know we are understood.
I think the Minister of Justice made an excellent case today, as he has on other occasions, for law reform, for strengthening our judiciary, for improving our parliamentary system and for all those other ways he has in mind to protect the rights of individual Canadians. Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock I was endeavouring to point out that our criticism of the bill which is before us arises from the fact that it fails to produce any measures which would protect our sovereignty and arrest the rapid drift toward foreign domination of our economy. I was seeking to make it clear that our objections were not based on any petty nationalism, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) has suggested.

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act Rather, we say that ownership implies the power to make decisions and that the decision-making power affecting the welfare of the people of this country, their jobs, their standard of living and their future, ought to be vested increasingly in the hands of bodies and organizations accountable and responsible to the people of Canada.
Those who are content to allow this drift toward continentalism to continue try to explain their inertia and inaction by contending that Canada cannot secure sufficient capital unless it allows these takeovers. This is one of the myths which was successfully exploded by the Watkins Commission. As a matter of fact, over the past ten years Canada has been an exporter of capital. In recent years we have been providing over $500 million a year to purchase equities in the United States, because most of the subsidiaries in Canada are wholly-owned United States subsidiaries which do not offer their shares to the Canadian public. Consequently, those who manage the investment for pension funds, insurance, mutual funds and the like find it necessary to go to the United States market to buy equities in order to balance their portfolios.
Moreover, it should be remembered that the capital which is being used to buy out Canadian companies comes largely from Canadians. Over the past ten years, only 15 per cent of the capital which is being used to take over Canadian companies has been new United States capital; the other 85 per cent is an accumulation of dividends and interest earned in Canada on previous investments. In other words, the people of Canada have supplied the capital necessary to permit the foreclosure of their own economy.
Adequate capital could be found in this country to develop the economy of Canada. Should it be necessary at any time to secure additional funds to enlarge our infrastructure, this could be done by going into the markets of the world to secure loan capital in the form of bonds and debentures where no ownership is involved. Once we pay off the interest and the principle, ownership rests entirely in Canadian hands. Surely there are sufficient savings generated by Canadian people to enable us to provide the major part, if not all of the capital we require for equity in the development of our economy. After all, during the second world war the Canadian people, rising out of a great depression, equipped nearly 1 million men and women in the armed services, built ships, tanks, guns
[Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
and planes, waged a war entirely out of Canadian resources and in addition gave very large sums of money to the United Kingdom to help that country in its hour of need.
Our problem would not be capital. The area in which we would really need foreign assistance would be that of technical knowhow, something which is much more difficult to secure. But this could be obtained, as Israel and other countries have done, by entering into partnership with foreign companies, allowing them to have a one-third equity, to supply the patents and in some cases to operate under management contracts. But we would retain control in Canada and keep the decision-making power in this country.
We in this party are disappointed that this legislation does not set out the steps the government intends to take to prevent a continuation of this growing takeover of the Canadian economy. We think there are steps which should be taken, some of them short term and immediate. For instance, we think there ought to be a takeover tax. A former Minister of Finance, Mr. Walter Gordon, did introduce legislation into this House providing for such a tax. Then, under pressure, he withdrew it. I am not in a position to say from whence the pressure came, but when Mr. Gordon writes his memoirs and we get another "Bird in a Gilded Cage", we shall know where it came from. Such a measure ought to be reintroduced. Many countries impose takeover taxes, and we need one in this country.
In the second place, there should be full disclosure of ownership so that we know the extent of foreign ownership of the various corporations in this country. Disclosure legislation will only be meaningful, however, if it is enforced. It will have to be better enforced than the legislation provided in the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act because in 1967, although 2,990 companies made no returns, no legal action was taken against them despite the fact that provision exists for taking such action.

Third, we need legislation restricting foreign ownership particularly in key sectors of the economy. An agency ought to be set up, as was recommended in the Watkins report, to investigate these takeovers and to make sure that the subsidiaries in this country are acting as good corporate citizens. Fourth, we need a state trading corporation, as was recommended in the Watkins report. There has been a problem with U.S. subsidiaries in this country which have refused to trade with Communist countries because the parent company in the United States might be prosecuted under the U.S. Trading with the Enemy Act. These subsidiaries have taken the position that they are subject to United States law, not Canadian law. This difficulty can be obviated, in one way at least, either by establishing a state trading corporation or by giving such trading powers to the existing Canadian commercial agency.
The fifth suggestion, which we have made from time to time, is that we ought to use a floating exchange rate. At the present time we are taking hard-earned United States dollars which we have earned to help our balance of payments position, and selling them for Canadian dollars to prevent the Canadian dollar going above the pegged rate. I suggest it would be difficult to find a more asinine situation. We in this group have for a long time advocated that a floating exchange rate, even operated within certain limits, would give the government greater freedom of movement in conducting its monetary policies.
There are other long-term measures, of course, that ought to be initiated by the government. First is the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation that the Liberal government has included in the Speech from the Throne in every session since 1963. It was left out of this session's Speech from the Throne, probably because the government felt there was a limit on how long it could kid the public. In spite of this, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) keeps saying that the corporation is coming. Personally, I will believe it when I see the legislation on the order paper. We want a publicly 21611-9
Canada Corporations Act financed and publicly controlled Canada Development Corporation that will make possible the mobilization of the savings of the Canadian people to be used for the purpose of developing Canada's resources, processing Canada's raw materials and developing and expanding Canada's economy.
The second long-term requirement is balancing our trade with imports from the United States, as well as shifting some of our purchases to countries that are prepared to trade for Canadian goods. One of our difficulties is that we are so completely dependent upon the U.S. market. As the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson said when asked whether the government would protest the United States presence in Viet Nam: When you depend on one country for 60 per cent of your trade, it is not easy to quarrel with them on a matter of this sort.
Because of our proximity to the United States and our long-standing relations with that country, the United States will always be our major customer. In all probability we will continue to be their major customer. But the steady imbalance in our payments position keeps us in a constantly inferior position in our dealings with that country.
My plea is that a young country like Canada must think in terms of centuries, not just in terms of decades. There is little value in rapid growth if the end result is economic dependency. Canada's future lies in developing secondary and tertiary industries that will provide jobs and more stable prices. For us to be a mere supplier of raw materials and energy resources is to relegate us permanently to an inferior level of economic performance. We can never have a society devoted to the greatest good for the greatest number if our economic decisions are made in a country other than Canada and in the interests of a country other than Canada. Even our political and cultural identity is being eroded. Certainly our economic sovereignty is already threatened.
We can hope some day to make corporate power responsible to the public interest of this country, but only if that power has its roots in Canada. When that corporate power is vested in another country and we have little or no control over it, increasingly we will become an economic colony of another nation. We may be better off, though even that is debatable; but we will not be a free and independent country.

Mr. Speaker, just recently I was shocked to read in the newspaper that trustees for two bankrupt estates in Montreal had to apply to the Quebec Superior Court for injunctions to prevent the liquidators of the Bank of Western Canada transferring over $3 million of the bank's money to the bankrupts through a company in Nassau controlled by one of the bankrupts. The machinations by which this might have been accomplished are many and involved. The saving action, of course, must now be under the bankruptcy laws, but the near defeat of Canadian creditors to the extent of over $3 million of the Bank of Western Canada's money gives some indication of the need to tighten corporate control.
The purpose of the proposed amendments to the Canada Corporations Act is to give Canadian shareholders in closely-held companies, and all shareholders in widely-held public companies greater protection in that the company and those who control it, commonly referred to as management, are required to provide investing shareholders with much more information on which to base their decisions whether to invest in it or, if they have invested, whether to continue their support of existing management.
Canada Corporations Act
Under this new legislation those who have a substantial interest in the company either by way of shares, 10 per cent or more, or as officers of the company, known as insiders, must disclose all dealings with their own shares by filing with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs what are called insider reports. Management must prepare and send to shareholders before the annual meeting detailed statements called information circulars, which presumably will have to show the benefit that any member of management may have received from the company or any subsidiary company, and describe the company's activities during the year and management's grounds for seeking re-election. These new sections also provide for some control on the solicitation of proxies, including the necessity to identify in the information circular those proposed for re-election or election as directors.
In 1967, Ontario introduced much the same protective provisions into the Ontario Corporations Act, most of which followed the New York State Act. This bill, while adopting a great deal of the Ontario legislation, has changed and enlarged some of the sections. Obviously the bill is hoped to be a Bill of Rights for investors. Certainly, some abuses will be prevented if potential manipulators know that shareholders are in a position to exercise a reasonable scrutiny of the company's affairs during the year and are informed of management's share ownership and dealings with the company prior to the annual meeting. The new provisions have certainly opened the door for scrutiny, but I suggest we should go further and turn on some lights so that shareholders may always see and understand what has gone on and the significance of it to them.
The drafters have avoided some unnecessary confusion by following much of the format of the Ontario act as to arbitrary time periods for compulsory filing and description of documents, for example, insider reports, information circulars and proxy solicitation. But although many of the sections are intended to have the same meaning, they are not identical in words. Surely, when there is uniformity of intention there should be greater uniformity of language. I suggest that the federal authorities consult their opposite numbers in Ontario to establish greater uniformity in terminology so that a shareholder who masters one set of rules will understand the other. This type of legislation, with its supporting regulations, is perhaps the most complicated and sophisticated of any Canadian

January 13, 1970
Canada Corporations Act law. If we are to protect the investors we must see that they, as well as management and those who enforce the legislation, understand it.

Because the legislation is new there could be uncertainty until legal decisions have supplied interpretations. If there was greater uniformity between the federal and Ontario acts, at least where the sections are intended to accomplish the same purpose the jurisprudence under one act would be of assistance in interpreting the other, and both could gain from the New York legal decisions.
This bill, as does the Ontario act, provides that insider reports must be filed and thus be available for examination by shareholders who have the knowledge and facilities to go to the registration office to extract the information. However, there will be many shareholders who do not know the information is available, or who perhaps would find it difficult and expensive to go to the proper office to obtain it. In fact, if every shareholder did so, the burden on the registration office would be intolerable. A provision should be added to the new sections which would provide that there must be attached to or included in the information circular a summary of the insider reports that have been filed so that all shareholders are brought up to date in respect of the insider trading before the annual meeting.
Although there is provision for disclosure of actual trading by insiders, the control should reach further and provide for similar disclosure in respect of options, shares pledged to brokers or other trustees, and any other indirect interest in shares by insiders either in the main company or in any subsidiary or related company. So, also, should insiders be precluded from dealing in shares for some days before any takeover bid becomes public knowledge. Penalties and a right of civil action should be provided for any breach of these provisions.
In the large companies of today management's right to solicit proxy votes is a powerful weapon. Abuses must be guarded against or the protection which we seek to give may be circumvented. The bill may appear to be a complete legislative triumph, but it should go further. We should take advantage of the recent review, by the Supreme Court of Ontario, of the Ontario sections in respect of solicitation and voting of proxies by management and prevent what was there disclosed to be an abuse, before it happens again.

In a case in which I was personally involved as counsel, Charlebois v. British International Finance, the company then had control of the Bank of Western Canada, management solicited proxies and at the same time implied by the information circular that management as a whole proposed to support the old board of directors. However, although management voted the proxies which it collected in favour of the old board, one or two powerful members of management voted their own shares for, and elected directors whom they caused to be nominated at the meeting without any prior notice. This was obviously a deception on those who had given their proxies to management. It was necessary for us, in that case, to go to the courts, and after a long and expensive hearing the court found that this was constructive fraud and granted an injunction prohibiting the new board taking office.
This loophole should be plugged. It would be better if the section were enlarged to provide that if management puts forward a list of directors, they must vote for those directors or the meeting is void. If an individual member of management wishes to oppose the board which the majority of management has agreed upon, and vote his shares for another, he should be required to so inform the shareholders.
The new sections provide that if insiders or certain others associated with the company should use their special knowledge of the company's affairs for their own trading gain, they are accountable to the company in legal action which may be taken by the department. I suggest this provision would have a greater restraining effect on those who would seek to gain improperly at the expense of others if in addition a group of shareholders could commence and conduct an action either in their own names or in the name of the company for the benefit of the company and thus indirectly for themselves.

I am sure these people are not the ones who are really concerned about the white paper. They are the people who really made the communities in bygone days. Now our whole community, our way of life and the social atmosphere in this society are impaired to the extent that the absentee owners make the decisions in Canada, and they are not really concerned about our economy. I am sure that with the passage of Bill C-4, this situation will not be changed. Hopefully, the reporting required will mean something to the people of Canada.
Let me refer to an article that appeared in the Toronto Star on November 11, 1969. It states:
A nationalism sigh of relief went up from many Canadians last spring when Rothmans of Pall Mall Canada beat U.S.-owned Philip Morris, another tobacco giant, for control of Canadian Breweries Ltd.
It was a good-guys-over-the-bad-guys feeling- a "hurrah for our side" cry. Canada had rallied and driven off the foreign invaders, many seemed to feel. They were dead wrong.
It was merely the victory of a South African based company over an America one. And it was symptomatic of a new trend in foreign ownership of Canada-a rise in the non-American share of our foreign-owned industries.
[Mr. Skoberg.l
To make the record very clear, once again let me say that this party has never deliberately campaigned to belittle our neighbours to the south. We have had to look to our neighbours to the south because of their tremendous input into our corporations and into the over-all control of our economy. We are now in a position where other countries are outdoing our neighbours to the south, and the same regulations must apply to them. I hope that any thought in anyone's mind that we are criticizing the United States will not persist. We want to know the source of this investment.
Let me quote from the bottom of page 705 of Hansard for November 10, 1969. The minister said:
Some people say that the government has the information it needs in its files, especially in the files of the Department of National Revenue, in the files of Calura and the Dominion Bureau of Statistics; that if it does not have the required information the government has the means of getting it. The claim is made, however, that there is no need to make public the information relative to the affairs of private companies; that to do so would amount to an unwarranted invasion of privacy.
I agree with the following sentence of the minister:
Those who speak that language surely do not appreciate all the implications of their position. I can hardly believe that in this day and age they want the government of the land to stand beyond the reach of the criticism of the citizens; that they want to allow the government of the land to take decisions that affect us all on the basis of information not available to the public. The public, even the otherwise well-informed public, the analysts, the academics and commentators, cannot appreciate, discuss or criticize policy as effectively as possible because of lack of access to the same information as is available to the policymakers or to the government.
If this government and the minister are sincere in respect of that statement, I hope the minister will stand in his place and provide answers or the information requested in many Notices of Motions for the Production of Papers. These motions really ask for the information which the minister recommends should be provided. He suggests the information will be made available as a result of this bill.
It has been suggested that the provisions of this measure will make this information public, through the press, and that in this way people requiring the information will obtain it. I have in mind the small investors who now receive no information. When the time comes, I feel that the minister will not be quick to jump to his feet to provide the
January 13, 1970

information to those people who want it. Before this debate is concluded I hope the minister will indicate that he agrees wholeheartedly that everything should be made public in order that everyone concerned may know what is going on.
Earlier I referred to the questionnaire that was sent out, in all sincerity, by many members. The answers contained in the majority of the 23,000 questionnaires sent out indicated a prime concern in respect of the control of our economy by foreign investors. When this bill goes to the committee I hope the minister will extend its term, in order that there may be real supervision of foreign investment. I am sure the Canadian people believe in Canada as a whole for Canadians. That is the position many people take in respect of this situation.
The primary method this government has of giving out information is undoubtedly through the Information Canada Service about which we have heard so much. I am wondering whether the minister's department will take advantage of this method in order to give the public the information required, or whether the public will have to pay for the information. Surely somewhere along the line this service should be made available to investors. This is one way in which we can make the general public more aware of what is taking place.
Some time ago the minister said there would be one change in the House regarding bills presented to us. At page 710 of Hansard for November 10 he referred to the method now used to handle the Canada Corporation Act and amendments, and said:
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The pressure of other business does not always permit the setting aside of sufficient parliamentary time to consider and dispose of requests for special acts to incorporate new companies or amend the original incorporating statutes. As a result, great inconvenience can at times be caused to the companies involved because of the uncertainty of the procedure and lengthy delays which are sometimes involved. We therefore propose an alternative procedure to the special act machinery.
It has been said many times in the House that members of this party have held up bills deliberately, without any justification. I should like to put on the record a letter one of our special assistants wrote to the editor and publisher of the Financial Post, dated April 21, 1969. It reads as follows:
Members of the NDP Caucus have been disturbed by your front page editorial-"Where a fix is badly needed"-March 1, 1969.
Canada Corporations Act
The New Democrats participating in the debate during private bills hour, are pursuing motives other than simple 'harrassment' as you have stated.

In addition to opposing further U.S. encroachment into the insurance business in Canada, the NDP members object to the proliferation of insurance companies-there are already more than 1,000 of them in this country-and to the subsequent diversion of more and more savings capital into private investment rather than into the financing of social needs."

It has never been proved that the more than 1,000 insurance companies have reduced their premiums. It has always been said that supply and demand will dictate the cost to the user, but today in any industry it would seem that the more companies there are, the more the price increases. If insurance companies were really competitive, one would wonder why premiums would not be reduced. I hope this measure is not merely windowdressing once again and an exercise in going

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-BILINGUALISM-USE OF INSTANT TRANSLATION COMPUTERS IN CLASSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked my question nearly two months ago. Having followed it through with some research I am convinced that it is even more important than it was at the time it was first asked. I have been reading some documents from the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, and my appraisal is further reinforced. Language is tremendously important in Canada today, both symbolically and realistically. Administrative efficiency is, of course, tremendously important in our times when the apparatus of the state is so powerful and its influence so pervasive.
I have always been an advocate of bilingualism in the government structure, but how we bilingualize institutions and departments of the government through the bilingualizing of individuals is a ques ion of great importance and great delicacy. Certainly government institutions should and must be bilingual, but what of the process whereby the individuals go through what we may describe as the bilingualizing course?
It is a great and valuable asset to know two languages, but it is very difficult for many people. Indeed, one of our finest neurologists pointed out that it was almost impossible for anyone past the age of puberty to become thoroughly and fully proficient in a language other than the original one. The process of bilingual training is very hard on many people who are doing hard and important
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion work in the service of the country. Perhaps it would be well to appraise the expenditure of time and effort and the laborious, difficult and often times, alas, unsuccessful immersion courses which many of our public servants are now taking. The sad part is that many who are immersed do not stay immersed, and this may well have deleterious effects upon their work output.
I will not dwell upon the emotional aspect of this question, the kind of thing which is stirred by the remark of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the running of elevators by unilingual people. But these things are involved. Nor will I dilate upon the great cost. I note a recent item which indicates that last year we spent $5,770,000 to give training to
5,000	employees of the government. So there is indeed a great cost involved. I was therefore delighted when I read the speech of that most excellent public servant, Mr. Gotlieb, Deputy Minister of the Department of Communications last fall when he spoke about the possibility of language computers which, in his words-
-can translate French to English and English to French. And the equipment has no inhibitions about who uses it.
We may soon reach the stage where telephones and television can be equipped with small, inexpensive translation computers that can instantly translate either of our official languages into the other.
I have read that one of the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State said that this happy state of affairs may be ten years away. But I wonder how far we are away from full, not to say perfect, thoroughgoing bilingualism. So the ten-year period does not upset me at all. It was once said by a great French philosopher that to govern is to foresee. I am sometimes dubious about the ability to foresee of the present government. But surely in an age where technology is so advanced and the acceleration of scientific development is still increasing, we must and should be alert to every opportunity to make the best use of modern technology for the best of national purposes.
I think that the rapid development of computerization in this field is something to which the government should give full attention as quickly as possible. I understand from financial institutions in the United States that great steps are being taken in this area.
I do not propose that we should expect miracles in a political institution, but perhaps this might be as close to a miracle solution of
January 13, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion an important matter as we are likely to reach. We all want full-fledged, functional bilingualism in this country. Institutions must and should be bilingual, and it must be achieved without pain to individuals and without developing a state where linguistic qualifications transcend all others. I believe the leading scientist in the government is going to reply to this question, and I would ask that urgent attention be given to this very important, potential breakthrough.

Mr. Speaker, the honourable and learned gentleman has raised questions on what he describes as the "foreseeability" of the present government. This, perhaps, is indicative of the problem which he has set the computers. I would defy him, and a number of other well-known forensic experts, to translate that expression in the exact sense he intended, that is, the question of the "foreseeability" of the present government.
I think this illustrates the nature of the problem. Language, French or perhaps even more particularly English, is capable of tremendous nuances, tremendous shades of meaning, part of which is conveyed by phonetics and inflections of speech, and part of which is conveyed by different pronunciations of different words spelled in the same way.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-BILINGUALISM-USE OF INSTANT TRANSLATION COMPUTERS IN CLASSES
speechtext: And by shrugs.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-BILINGUALISM-USE OF INSTANT TRANSLATION COMPUTERS IN CLASSES
speechtext:
Part of the meaning is conveyed in the order in which the same words are used. As yet we have not found a computer, even the largest, capable of programming, comprehending and producing all these shades and nuances which the human brain- perhaps the world's greatest computer-has been able to achieve in a number of instances.
For some time now the National Research Council has been supporting research work at the universities of Saskatchewan and Montreal, designed to produce a reasonable and practicable system of machine-translation from English into French. The hon. gentleman is probably well aware that considerable additional work is being done in this field, particularly in the United States, in languages rather less mundane than English and French-some of the eastern European languages and some Asiatic languages-but to date no one has achieved more than a rudimentary system of translation. This, of course, has to be extensively edited by a human computer or a person trained in translation.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
I think it is rather more likely that we will reach a level of bilingualism in primary, secondary and higher education in this country which will be more widely effective and more usable than the kind of machine program indicated here. We can now and in the reasonable future will be able to do primitive work, if nothing sophisticated.

subsubtopic: BROADCASTING-EFFECT OF CRTC DECISION RESPECTING CABLEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this participation in the adjournment debate arises out of my dissatisfaction with an answer given me by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) as reported at page 92 of the English edition of Hansard of December 17. The question was a follow-up of questioning by myself and other members, on December 4, reported at pages 1587 and 1588 of Hansard, concerning the ruling announced on December 3 by the Canadian Radio-Television Commission denying the use of microwave or other technical systems for the importation of television programs from United States stations to Canadian markets.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Effectively, the ruling denies access to United States television for Canadians living too far from the United States border to receive the signal off the air, either directly or via community antenna television systems. This does not affect Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal. It does deny United States television to Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, Saskatoon, Sudbury, Halifax and St. John's. No Canadian will dispute that the Canadian broadcasting system envisaged by the Broadcasting Act is essential to our national identity. Most will dispute that geographic discrimination has a valid place in the development of that policy.
The CRTC expressed concern about enlarging United States advertising markets in Canada. That consideration is purely fatuous. The CRTC is, or should be, well aware that it is entirely within the competence of today's technology to delay the signal and edit out the bulk of the commercial content. The advertising aspects of this competition can be readily resolved. The sanctity of the idea that cablevision must transmit the signal, the whole signal, and nothing but the signal, was destroyed on June 25, 1968, when cablevision companies were required to delete the eastern
January 13, 1970

election results from United States signals distributed in Vancouver while the polls were still open there.
In reaching its decision, the CRTC determined, "The fact that through force of circumstances many U.S. stations now cover other parts of Canada ... does not justify a decision... which would further accelerate this process." The corollary of this position is: the fact that through force of circumstances many parts of Canada are not now covered by U.S. stations justifies a decision which would perpetuate this situation.
It is with considerable trepidation that an ordinary Canadian enters into the never-never world of the professional Canadian. But I am compelled to ask, does the CRTC really feel that it is serving the national interest by creating yet another division in an already overly-divided Canada: those who should be permitted access to U.S. stations because a fact of geography prevents the CRTC from denying such access, and those who shall be denied access to U.S. stations because a fact of geography permits the CRTC to deny such access? While the question of which are the first class citizens and which the second may be open to dispute by the professional Canadians, there is no doubt in so far as those who have been denied a right on purely geographic grounds are concerned.
Section 2(b) of the Broadcasting Act reads as follows:
-the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada;
It is in the execution of its mandate to achieve and maintain this basic purpose-and let it be emphasized that while "safeguard" embraces the concept of maintenance, "enrich and strengthen" embrace the concept of achievement-that the CRTC must justify its decision.
If, in the process of safeguarding the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada, the CRTC is right in refusing a licence permitting "the enlargement of the Canadian audience and market areas of U.S. networks or stations" then surely, in the process of enriching and strengthening the same fabric, its obligation is to reduce the same audience and market areas where it can. This will involve the simple policy of not renewing existing CATV licences as they expire, except on condition that the applicants not distribute U.S. programs. Let us not only prevent the extension of this rupture in our cultural,
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion political, social and economic fabric; let us also mend it where we can. Let us not only preserve the fabric where it remains intact; let us patch it where it has been torn. Let us not only safeguard the pure; let us enrich and strengthen those already corrupted.
When the Secretary of State first answered questions on this subject on December 4, I felt his instincts were right. He indicated that the decision "could very well justify a statement on motions" and, again, that the CRTC's autonomy did not prevent the government giving it guidelines. This instinctive reaction was the right reaction. It was, therefore, particularly disappointing to find, on December 17, that the minister had got his instincts well under control and was relying on the letter of the law. The commission is independent, and cannot be instructed by the government.
This ruling has profound political implications. It is the government, not the CRTC, that will be held politically accountable for the decision. Surely, with the adventures of another independent body, the Company of Young Canadians, rather fresh in its memory, the government recognizes that reality.
We were pretty happy with the work of the CYC in Calgary. That opinion was not shared in Montreal, and for very good reason. As far as I know, Montreal is reasonably happy with the CRTC. That opinion is not shared in Calgary, and for very good reason. Nor is it shared in Edmonton, Regina, Saskatoon, Sudbury, Halifax and St. John's for the same good reason.
We are all awaiting with interest to see if the government will react with the same vigour to the politically unacceptable conduct of the independent commission as it did to that of the independent company, or whether it has certain geographic priorities of its own.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has observed, the Canadian Radio-Television Commission is an independent body established under the Broadcasting Act to supervise and ensure the development of the Canadian broadcasting system, free of partisan political control. If that act should be amended, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) would welcome the suggestions of hon. members. However, the Broadcasting Act, section 23, allows the Governor in Council to set aside or refer back to the commission for reconsideration its decision to issue, amend or renew a broadcasting licence, but there is no such authority in the case of a rejection of an

subsubtopic: COMBINES-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF NICKEL PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 27 I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) whether the anti-combines division of his department would investigate the simultaneous increases in the price of nickel announced within two days by three of the major nickel producers of this country.
My question was motivated by the very sharp increase in the price of metals produced and sold in Canada and the disastrous effect these increases will have on the government's plea to all sectors of the Canadian economy that they exercise moderation and restraint so that the galloping increase in the cost of living might be moderate.
The Financial Times of January 5, 1970, reported that the price of lead in 1969 increased by 27 per cent; the price of nickel increased 24 per cent; zinc, 15 per cent; tin, 12 per cent; aluminum, 7 per cent and copper, about which we had some considerable discussion this afternoon, increased by 26 per cent. This does not include the latest increase which was announced and which the government persuaded the companies to put off for two months. This will increase the price of copper by 45 per cent in one year.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
What happened? On October 25 the International Nickel Company of Canada announced that nickel prices were being increased by a record 24.8 per cent. Inco's
fMr. Stanbury.]
new price for electrolytic refined metal was $1.28 (U.S.) per pound, up $1.03 (U.S.) per pound. Sherritt Gordon, another of the major producers, matched Inco's 25 cents a pound increase for nickel sold in the United States and overseas but raised its Canadian price by 23 cents a pound. The next day the third large producer, Falconbridge, completed the round of nickel price increases when it raised the base price of electrolytic nickel by 25 cents (U.S.) to $1.27 (U.S.) a pound f.o.b. Thorold.
The district organization of the United Steelworkers, the union which represents all the workers employed in the mining and processing of nickel, called on the Prices and Incomes Commission to hold a public hearing, offering to demonstrate on the basis of the research done by the union's research department that the companies' profits were so substantial there was no need to increase prices as they had done.
Industries affected were quick to announce that the sharp increases would inevitably and almost immediately lead to increases in their prices. Mr. Togham, President of Chrysler Canada Limited said-and this is reported in the Globe and Mail of October 26-that the 25 cent price increase in the metal was bound to increase the price of cars. Similarly, Mr. O.S. Leslie, President of Atlas Steels Limited, probably the biggest domestic user of nickel, said the new price increase was certain to have an effect on the cost and price of stainless steel.
I want to put on record the financial position of the companies concerned. One can find these figures in the Financial Post. The net income of International Nickel in 1967 was $141 million. In 1968 it showed a modest increase to $143 million, but the total assets had grown from $115 million to $396 million; in other words, by about $275 million in one year. This is a pretty substantial increase and one which does not indicate any need on the part of this company to increase its price by 24 per cent at one time.
Sherritt Gordon's net profit in 1966 amounted to $3,760,000. In the next year it had increased to $5,392,000, and I am sure 1968 showed a further increase. The net income of the Falconbridge Corporation dropped a little in 1968 as compared with 1967, from $25 million to $23 million. But the total assets increased from $248 million to $284 million, a substantial increase and one which would indicate that this company, too,
January 13. 1970	COMMONS
could very well have done without an increase at the time announced.
What I am saying is simply this: the anticombines section of the hon. gentleman's department should exercise the responsibility given to it by the law to investigate these simultaneous and identical price increases, which in my submission indicate clearly that we have here a combine in any sense of the word and one which ought to be prosecuted to the end of obtaining an order to discontinue the kind of collusion which is obvious in the price increases announced in October, 1969.
